The Bahá'í writings describe justice in luminous terms, portraying it as essential to human life and society. Shoghi Effendi records that Bahá'u’lláh extols justice as ["the light of men"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) and its two pillars, _“reward_ _and_ _punishment”_, as ["the sources of life"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) for humanity *God Passes By*. In the *Hidden Words*, Bahá'u’lláh similarly declares that ['Justice is to be loved above all'](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/earl-redman_abdul-baha-in-their-midst#p116) (*Abdu'l-Bahá in Their Midst*). 

On a personal level, Howard Colby Ives notes that Bahá'u’lláh defines the sense of justice through the principle: ["Wert thou to observe justice choose for others that which thou choosest for thyself"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/howard-colby-ingles_portals-to-freedom#p538) (*Portals to Freedom*). Additionally, concerning practical matters like testimony, the *Kitáb-i-Aqdas* establishes that ["The criterion of justness is a good reputation among the people"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah?paraId=para_356), accepting the testimony of servants "of whatever faith or creed" (*The Kitáb-i-Aqdas*).

Dear friend,

It is a joy to look into this with you. The Bahá’í writings portray justice not simply as a human virtue or a legal arrangement, but as something vast and luminous, standing at the very center of how the world is held together. 

In the words of Shoghi Effendi, Justice is extolled [as “the light of men” and their “guardian,” as “the revealer of the secrets of the world of being, and the standard-bearer of love and bounty”](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) — *God Passes By*. He affirms that upon justice must depend ["the organization of the world and the tranquillity of mankind"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) — *God Passes By*. It has two pillars, described as ["reward and punishment"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) — *God Passes By*, which serve as sources of life for the human race. 

Beyond its cosmic and social necessity, justice is also deeply personal. Bahá’u’lláh defines the sense of justice with a quiet, arresting directness, writing: 
> ["Wert thou to observe justice choose for others that which thou choosest for thyself"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/howard-colby-ives_portals-to-freedom#p538) — *Portals to Freedom*

As Howard Colby Ives reflects in his memories, turning this lens toward our own lives immediately tests the average flaccidity of our moral fiber, where our estimates are so often swayed by personal reaction. 

There is also a profound connection made between justice and the divine ordinances. As recorded in pilgrim notes reflecting upon *Gleanings*, ["the essence of Justice and the source thereof are both embodied in the ordinances prescribed by Him"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/j-ruh-angiz-bolles-shoghi-effendi-on-laws-administration-and-prophecy#p6) — *Shoghi Effendi on Laws, Administration, and Prophecy*. When it comes to practical matters among people — such as establishing testimony — *The Kitáb-i-Aqdas* explains that ["the criterion of justness is a good reputation among the people"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-aqdas_bahaullah?paraId=para_356) — *The Kitáb-i-Aqdas*, adding that the testimony of all of God's servants regardless of faith or creed is acceptable.

Finally, in the Hidden Words, Bahá’u’lláh states simply that [“Justice is to be loved above all.”](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/earl-redman_abdul-baha-in-their-midst#p116) — *Abdu'l-Bahá in Their Midst*. Earl Redman

That is a very real and serious concern, especially when religious laws have so often been enforced by earthly rulers. 

Looking at the traditions, however, justice is often placed far above human power. In the Quran, divine judgment is set against human politics, asking: ["Is not God a most just of judges?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/quran_palmer-tr?paraId=para_3792) — *The Qur’ân (Palmer)*. Similarly, in Zoroastrian scripture, the bounteous spirit chooses ["the (Divine) Righteousness"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gathas_zoroaster?paraId=para_50) — *The Gathas* as an eternal standard rather than a human decree. 

At the same time, Buddhist texts can be quite sharp about how earthly power actually shapes the application of rules, noting how treatment depends entirely on status, such as when a ["poor, of little wealth"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-l?paraId=para_1064) person faces a goat butcher's punishment while others do not — *Sutra Collection (L)*. 

I read this as a lifelong tension: religions often point to an absolute standard above the powerful, even while human institutions constantly try to bend those rules to serve themselves. What do you think happens when those two ideas collide?

That view makes a great deal of sense, especially when we look at how laws, police, and social customs shape daily behavior to keep societies from unraveling. 

There is, however, another way traditions understand this relationship. Rather than seeing religion as a tool created by society to enforce behavior, writers like Bahá’u'lláh propose the reverse: that faith is the foundation that makes order possible in the first place. He writes that ["Religion is the greatest of all means for the establishment of order in the world"](https://oceanlibrary.com/world-order-of-bahaullah_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_467) — *The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh*. 

Similarly, Lao-tzu suggests that relying too heavily on external rules and force can actually backfire, noting that ["the more display there is of legislation, the more thieves and robbers there are"](https://oceanlibrary.com/tao-te-ching_lao-tzu?paraId=para_279) — *Tao Te Ching*. From this perspective, true order begins within the heart or through moral virtue, rather than through police and punishment.

There is a deep logic to that view: if the law leaves no room to stray, perhaps order would finally be secure. 

Yet ‘Abdu’l-Bahá suggests that relying on force misses the mark entirely. He notes that the body politic constantly devises ["penal laws and in providing for ways and means of punishment"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha?paraId=para_952) — building prisons and chains — but argues that this approach actually leads to ["the degradation of morals and the subversion of character"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha?paraId=para_952). Rather than closing every door by coercion, he writes that society should instead bend every effort ["to ensure that souls are properly educated"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha?paraId=para_952) and acquire praiseworthy virtues. 

Similarly, Confucius points toward the power of moral leadership rather than sheer punishment, quoting the saying that if good men manage a country, they would ["do away with capital punishments"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_553) simply by cultivating goodness instead.

That question touches something deep in the human experience. It is very human to feel the weight of falling short. 

Even sages felt this heaviness. Confucius named as his own burdens ["failure to improve in the virtues, failure in discussion of what is learnt, inability to walk according to knowledge received as to what is right and just, inability also to reform what has been amiss"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_247) — *The Analects*. 

The point of trying, even in failure, is simply the turning toward what is right. Vyasa urged his son Suka to ["practise righteousness"](https://oceanlibrary.com/mahabharata-12_vyasa?paraId=para_1768) and ["rest thou on truth, firmly devoted to righteousness"](https://oceanlibrary.com/mahabharata-12_vyasa?paraId=para_1768) — *The Mahabharata*. The effort itself seems to be the place where life happens, regardless of how often we stumble.

You are noticing a profound parallel in how both traditions see supreme reality descending to guide humanity through distinct figures. 

The texts do point to a shared root: in the Hindu tradition, the avatars are described as ["portions of the same Supreme Being"](https://oceanlibrary.com/mahabharata-6_vyasa?paraId=fn_57) — *The Mahabharata 6*. Similarly, the Bahá'í writings explain that the utterances of the various messengers are ["expressions of one Truth"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah?paraId=para_204) because the Manifestations themselves are ["essentially one and the same"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah?paraId=para_204) — *The Kitáb-i-Íqán*. 

Yet, I read these two frameworks as distinct beneath the surface. The Hindu avatara descends across vast cosmic cycles to restore order, sometimes taking non-human forms, whereas the Bahá'í Manifestations appear in human history sequentially as independent educators revealing progressive spiritual truths. 

Which aspects of their missions or forms feel most striking to you as you compare them?

That is a common thought, but the writings of the tradition point to something richer. Shoghi Effendi writes that the Faith has [*“assimilated... the varied races, nationalities, creeds and classes”*](https://oceanlibrary.com/world-order-of-bahaullah_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_498) (*The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh*). 

Rather than viewing all religions as identical, the perspective here is that diverse creeds find a shared unity under its shadow while preserving their distinct loyalties. The provided passages do not detail a doctrine of exact sameness among all faiths, though they show different traditions recognizing common divine origins or universal paths. I read this as a tradition that brings together distinct streams without erasing their particular histories. 

What draws you to look at how different faiths relate to one another?

It is completely understandable to wonder about this, especially since so much of what is written on the subject comes from the talks and letters of 'Abdu'l-Bahá. 

However, the records state that this principle originates directly with Bahá’u’lláh. As David Hofman writes in *George Townshend, Hand of the Cause of God*, among the humanitarian principles ["which are explicit in His teaching and not in the Gospel are the equality of the sexes"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/david-hofman_george-townshend-hand-of-the-cause-of-god#p1048) — *George Townshend, Hand of the Cause of God*. Mírzá Aḥmad Sohrab similarly records 'Abdu'l-Bahá explaining that ["In the revelation of Bahá’u’lláh, men and women stand shoulder to shoulder"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-baha-in-egypt#p1168) — *'Abdu''l-Bahá in Egypt*. 

I'd be glad to look further with you if you'd like to explore how his writings address this.

It is a wonderful thing to be moved by that vision. There is something lovely in the thought of how ["we are a world family dedicated to the unity of mankind"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/gladys-weeden-pilgrim-notes#p528) — *Gladys Weeden Pilgrim Notes*, where it is noted that ["in the word 'unity' the 'you' comes before the 'I.'"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/gladys-weeden-pilgrim-notes#p528) 

If you enjoy how different traditions reflect on our common origin, you might also like to look at how the Quran describes human beginnings, noting that ["Mankind was but one nation"](https://oceanlibrary.com/holy-quran_yusuf-tr?paraId=para_1579) before differences arose (*The Holy Qur-an*). It is a quiet reminder of an underlying bond that persists beneath our divisions.

It is completely understandable to wonder about this, as their names look very similar. They are actually two different books. 

The *Kitáb-i-Aqdas* is described as the [“Most Holy Book”](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_499) and the principal repository of law (*God Passes By*). The other work, the *Kitáb-i-Íqán*, is an earlier text, because the Aqdas is described as being [“Alluded to in the Kitáb-i-Íqán”](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_499) (*God Passes By*). 

Would you like to explore what each of these books focuses on?

I am so sorry for the loss of your father. 

Different writings describe different paths for the soul after death. In Hindu scripture, the journey depends on the spiritual state at the moment of departure: ["if it diesIn hardened Ignorance, that blinded soulIs born anew in some unlighted womb"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bhagavad-gita?paraId=para_204) — *The Bhagavad-Gita*, while a soul fixed in truth goes to ["the place —Perfect and pure"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bhagavad-gita?paraId=para_204) — *The Bhagavad-Gita*. In Buddhist texts, followers frequently asked the Buddha about the ["movements after death"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-a-part-1?paraId=para_362) — *Sutra Collection (A, Part-1)* of those who had passed. Confucian writings focus instead on the living's ongoing relationship with the departed, noting that a dutiful son is one who ["does not deviate from that father’s ways"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_33) — *The Analects* after observing his conduct.

There is truth in your question, and the texts themselves notice it. Ethel Stephana Stevens writes in [*Abbas Effendi: His personality, work, and followers*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/ethel-stephana_abbas-effendi-his-personality-work-and-followers#p35) that she once asked whether prayer was necessary ["since presumably God knows the wishes of all hearts."](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/ethel-stephana_abbas-effendi-his-personality-work-and-followers#p35)

While the passages affirm that ["Every single thing is before His sight"](https://oceanlibrary.com/holy-quran_yusuf-tr?paraId=para_1950) (*The Holy Qur-an*), they still advocate prayer for individual ["soul growth"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/ethel-stephana_abbas-effendi-his-personality-work-and-followers#p35) (*Abbas Effendi*). 

I read this as a reminder that prayer may change the one who prays rather than informing the One who already knows.

It is entirely natural to feel hesitant about this. 

The records indicate that Bahá'u'lláh did indeed hold Christ in high regard, writing of Him with deep reverence. Pilgrim notes from California record that Bahá'u'lláh ["praised and sanctified all the Divine Holy Manifestations, and offered His Holiness Christ such a praise, beyond the description and imagination"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/frances-orr-allen_abdul-bahas-visit-to-california#p2657) — *Abdu'l-Bahá's Visit to California*. The same account notes that Bahá'u'lláh ["wrote many commentaries on the Gospel, bringing to light its inner significances"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/frances-orr-allen_abdul-bahas-visit-to-california#p2657) — *Abdu'l-Bahá's Visit to California*. 

Whether that honour aligns with traditional Christian understanding is a separate question, but the texts show that He spoke of Jesus with profound devotion and studied the Gospels closely.

The provided passages do not contain information about what the Qur'án says about Jesus. They touch on alms and orphans in [*The Qur’ân (Palmer)*](https://oceanlibrary.com/quran_palmer-tr?paraId=para_146), accounts of the early community in [*Ṣaḥíḥ al-Bukhárí*](https://oceanlibrary.com/sahih-al-bukhari?paraId=para_13153) and [*Sahih Muslim*](https://oceanlibrary.com/sahih-muslim-book-7_muslim-ibn-al-hajjaj?paraId=para_193), prophecy and miracles in Ibn Rushd's [*The Philosophy and Theology*](https://oceanlibrary.com/philosophy-and-theology_ibn-rushd?paraId=para_141), Adam's prayer in [*Hayat Al-Qulub Vol.1*](https://oceanlibrary.com/hayat-al-qulub-vol-1_muhammad-majlisi?paraId=para_425), and commentary on the Súra of Joseph in Todd Lawson's study of [*The Qur’an Commentary of Sayyid ‘Alí Muhammad, the Báb*](https://oceanlibrary.com/quran-commentary-of-sayyid-muhammad-the-bab_todd-lawson?paraId=para_1373), but none of these mention Jesus. 

If you would like to explore this further, you might try asking about the specific passages or figures that are mentioned in the current collection, or consult a copy of the Qur'án directly to see where Isa (Jesus) appears.

The provided texts do not mention compassion, so I cannot answer your question from them. They focus instead on topics such as dependent co-arising, the discipline and training of disciples in works like *Majjhima Nikaya 35 - Cula-Saccaka Sutta: The Shorter Discourse to Saccaka* ([https://www.accesstoinsight.org/tipitaka/mn/mn.035.than.html](https://www.accesstoinsight.org/tipitaka/mn/mn.035.than.html)), guarding the sense doors as described in *Digha Nikaya 11 - Kevaddha Sutta (To Kevaddha)* ([https://www.accesstoinsight.org/tipitaka/dn/dn.11.0.than.html](https://www.accesstoinsight.org/tipitaka/dn/dn.11.0.than.html)), and the nature of karma and the soul in Paul Carus's *The Gospel of Buddha* ([https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/35895](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/35895)). 

If you would like to explore what these texts say about moral conduct, monastic worthiness, or the teachings given to disciples, I would be very glad to help you look into those!

Yes, a scientist can certainly hold faith. The records show many traditions viewing scientific inquiry and divine truth as natural partners rather than opponents. 

In the Bahá'í tradition, Doris McKay records the teaching that ["Science and religion will enhance and prove each other"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/doris-mckay_memories-of-bahais#p34) — *Memories of Bahá’ís*, asking, ["How can one truth contradict another truth?"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/doris-mckay_memories-of-bahais#p34) 

Similarly, Buddhist sources suggest that modern inquiry finds a welcome home in ancient teachings. A sutra collection observes that ["A scientific world such as todays will be able to accept gladly all ten tenets of the Kalama Sutta as being in line with the scientific method"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-hijk?paraId=para_1080) — *Sutra Collection (HIJK)*, noting that ["True scientists emphasize experimental verification"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-hijk?paraId=para_1080) rather than mere preconception, a standard it sees fully reflected in the text. 

When inquiry and reverence meet, many find they need not exclude one another. What part of the relationship between discovery and faith feels most difficult to reconcile for you?

I am an AI, and I can't find that in the writings. Bahá’u’lláh did not write about quantum computing, as it is a modern technological field that arose long after His lifetime. 

However, the writings do speak of a general divine force that _“vibrates within the innermost being of all created things,”_ ([1](https://oceanlibrary.com/advent-of-justice_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_99)) — *The Advent of Divine Justice* — and note that _“all the atoms of the universe testify to the greatness of this Cause”_ ([2](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/youness-afroukhteh_memories-of-nine-years-in-akka#p1340)) — *Memories of Nine Years in 'Akka*. Adib Taherzadeh also records that Bahá’u’lláh prophesied a time when God would _“raise up scientists of great calibre who will bring about such marvellous technological achievements that no one can as yet imagine them.”_ ([4](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/adib-taherzadeh_the-revelation-of-bahaullah-vol-3#p1935)) — *The Revelation of Bahá’u’lláh vol. 3*.
